items.text: Sequence matters more than most self-taught roadmaps admit.
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the floor, not the roadmap.
None of these four layers exist in isolation.
"Full stack" gets thrown around loosely, but Indian job postings are fairly consistent about what they actually expect across these four layers.
Learn plain JavaScript deeply enough to explain what React is doing under the hood, closures, the event loop, and array methods, before you lean on a framework to hide the gaps.
Variables, functions, array methods, async/await, and the DOM.
Pick React (or your chosen framework) and build one real, deployed project with it, routing, forms, state management, and at least one API call, before moving to the backend.
Every stack below can genuinely get you hired in India.

The most common full-stack pairing in Indian startup and product-company job postings, largely because it lets you stay in one language across the frontend and backend, which shortens the learning curve and the codebase context-switching.
You want the fastest realistic path into startups, SaaS companies, and product teams, and you are comfortable learning JavaScript deeply enough to use it on both ends.
Starting React, Node, MongoDB, Docker, and a cloud platform in the same week produces shallow exposure to all of them and real competence in none.
Following along with a video builds recognition, not recall.
A project sitting only on your laptop is not proof of work a recruiter can verify in ten seconds.

rows: A live link a recruiter can click matters more than a paragraph describing features. Candidates who can point to deployed projects consistently move through screening faster than those who only list technologies.
A GitHub profile that reads like real work

Meaningful commit history, a clear README with setup instructions and the tech stack used, and code that is not one giant unformatted file all signal that you can work inside a real codebase, not just finish a tutorial.
One project with real authentication and a real database

To-do list clones without login systems or with hardcoded fake data are the most common junior portfolio filler. A project with real signup, real sessions or tokens, and real persisted data stands out precisely because it is less common.
Comfort explaining trade-offs, not just syntax

Interviewers increasingly ask why you chose MongoDB over a relational database, or why you structured an API a certain way, not just whether you can recite syntax. This is where actually building projects beats memorising documentation.
Being able to explain your own deployment setup, read your own error logs, and show a clean commit history signals you can survive outside a guided course environment.

items.text: Connect a real database and handle the messy parts: pagination, relationships between records, and what your app does when a query fails, not just the happy path where everything works.
Deploy every project, even the small ones.
Pick at least one project around a problem you genuinely care about, even a small local one, instead of cloning the same e-commerce or to-do app template everyone else builds.
Wider hiring pool: startups and small product teams often want one person who can own a feature end to end.
You can ship an entire idea alone, useful for freelancing, side projects, or early-stage startup roles.
Salary at the fresher and mid level is often slightly ahead of a single-layer specialist, because you cover more ground.
The trade-off: depth suffers if you never go deep on any one layer, and senior full-stack roles still expect real depth somewhere.
Clean Git history, a working Dockerfile, and a deployed live URL.
A large share of MERN-based job postings in India now expect TypeScript.
